reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: Caused by absence of the bony roof over the superior semicircular canal, creating a pathological 'third window' into the labyrinth
Sound- or pressure-induced vertigo and oscillopsia (Tullio phenomenon and Hennebert sign) are characteristic and often triggered by loud noise, coughing or straining
Autophony (hearing one's own voice, heartbeat, or eye movements unusually loudly) is a common and distressing symptom
Audiometry classically shows a low-frequency air-bone gap with intact or supranormal bone conduction, mimicking conductive loss despite a normal mobile ossicular chain
Cervical and ocular vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials (VEMPs) show abnormally low thresholds and enlarged amplitudes on the affected side
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone with reformats in the planes of the superior canal (Poschl and Stenver views) confirms the bony defect
Many radiographically thin or dehiscent canals are asymptomatic, so imaging must be correlated with symptoms and physiology before intervention
Symptomatic cases may be managed conservatively or by surgical canal plugging or resurfacing via a middle-fossa or transmastoid approach
reference.pathophysiology: The superior semicircular canal normally lies enclosed within dense bone beneath the floor of the middle cranial fossa. When this bony covering is congenitally thin or eroded, a dehiscence creates an abnormal 'third mobile window' in addition to the oval and round windows. Acoustic and pressure energy that would normally drive the cochlea is instead partly shunted through the dehiscence, abnormally stimulating the vestibular apparatus and dissipating sound energy. This explains sound- and pressure-evoked vertigo, the low-frequency pseudo-conductive hearing pattern with preserved bone conduction, autophony, and the hypersensitive VEMP responses.
additionalDifferentials: Otosclerosis or other causes of a conductive air-bone gap
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution temporal bone CT with Poschl and Stenver reformats
Pure-tone audiometry with masked bone conduction to demonstrate the low-frequency air-bone gap
Cervical and ocular vestibular-evoked myogenic potential testing
Tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing to show a mobile ossicular chain with preserved reflexes
Video-oculography to document the vertical-torsional nystagmus evoked by sound or pressure
redFlags: Disabling vertigo or oscillopsia interfering with daily function or driving
Symptoms suggesting a coexisting intracranial process such as raised intracranial pressure or an encephalocoele through the defect
Progressive sensorineural hearing loss beyond the expected pseudo-conductive pattern
New cerebrospinal fluid leak or meningitic features
reference.prognosis: Many patients have mild symptoms that can be managed conservatively by avoiding provoking stimuli. When symptoms are disabling, surgical plugging or resurfacing of the canal relieves sound- and pressure-induced vestibular symptoms in most cases, though there is a small risk of hearing loss and symptoms may occasionally recur or arise on the contralateral side.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the low-frequency air-bone gap as otosclerosis and performing unnecessary stapes surgery
Relying on CT alone, since thin or dehiscent bone is common and may be asymptomatic or overcalled by volume averaging
Overlooking autophony and pulsatile or self-sound symptoms that point to a third-window disorder
Failing to counsel about the small operative risk to hearing before canal surgery
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Manage mild symptoms conservatively by avoiding provoking loud sounds, pressure changes and straining
Offer surgical plugging, capping or resurfacing of the superior canal via a middle fossa or transmastoid approach for disabling sound- and pressure-induced symptoms
Consider round window reinforcement as a less invasive surgical alternative
Provide vestibular rehabilitation to aid compensation for imbalance
Counsel on the small risk of hearing loss and symptom recurrence associated with surgery
Monitor with audiometry and vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials and refer to a neurotology service
